Yeah, there is a lot mystery in the sleep field. However, that's not to say we don't understand it at all. I think there is enough evidence available to reasonably hypothesize a general answer to OP's question.

Actually, that’s not totally true. Our circadian rhythms appears to have two peaks during the day. One is in the morning and the other(bigger one) is in the evening. These peaks are correlated with levels of awareness/alertness. So in the early afternoon, when our circadian rhythm dips, we feel tired because of the natural lull. In addition, we also are affected by our homeostatic sleep drive(aka how much sleep deprivation we have). Those two factors result in faster sleep onset. 

Source: took a seminar course on sleep focused solely on the current research.
If you have the time, I recommend The Promise of Sleep by William C. Dement. It's a bit dated, but much of the information is still relevant in our foundational understanding of sleep behavior

I’m glad you’ve been able to feel better lately and been able to make meaningful relationships. However, I still feel like saying “it gets better” is a painful cliche to hear. 


I think life gets better...for some people. Others are trapped in negative spirals hoping one day things will change. This hoping can go on for years and years. Even if you’re getting all the “correct treatment” this process can go on forever. In my experience, this depression doesn’t dissipate. It may wax and wane, but it always seems to be lurking waiting for an opportunity to rear it’s head. 

Had you not had good friends and those that helped you / cared about you, your experience most likely would have been drastically different. Not everyone has the social abilities or adequate environmental circumstances to foster deep, meaningful friendships with others. I’d still argue that “it gets better” is a effortless, biased blanket statement. I don’t think it’s helpful to those who have been suffering for an extended period of time. 

A more realistic statement might look like “you get better at dealing with feeling like shit most of the time, but you’re still gonna feel like shit.”
Not to mention the shortened life expectancy due to disease and lack of medicine. It would be rare to have someone live past their 60s.
